html:
A paved trackway across the Isthmus of Corinth, about 6 to 8 km long, on which ships and cargo were hauled between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf. It was built around 600 BCE, perhaps under the tyrant Periander.

The road was made of limestone blocks with grooves to guide wheeled carts. It saved ships the long and dangerous voyage around the Peloponnese. It mostly carried goods, and the tolls made Corinth rich. In wartime it also moved warships, as in the Peloponnesian War, when Sparta and its allies dragged fleets across.

It stayed in use for centuries, at least into the 1st century CE. The emperor Nero started digging a real canal in 67 CE but gave up. The Corinth Canal was finally cut in 1893, close to the old track, and parts of the Diolkos can still be seen beside it.
sum: A paved trackway across the Isthmus of Corinth, about 6 to 8 km long, on which ships and cargo were hauled between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf. It was built around 600 BCE, perhaps under the tyrant Periander.
